summary: Ehrman narrowly prevailed by proving consequential local misattributions, while White strongly defended recoverable textual and theological continuity.

pro.context: Ehrman closes by focusing on the manuscripts Christians actually used, arguing that scribal mistakes in transmitted words of Jesus make historical Bibles locally misattribute wording.

con.context: White closes by distinguishing copying differences from false quotation, grounding his denial in recoverable apostolic teaching and continuity of Jesus’s message across the manuscript tradition.

moves.words: Successive hand copies inherited earlier mistakes, introduced additional ones, and eventually lost the exemplars needed to identify every original word.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman supplies a concrete cumulative mechanism in which inherited alterations, fresh copying errors, attempted corrections, and disappearing exemplars jointly explain why mere survival does not authenticate every word. Principal limitation: the illustrative chain is deliberately simplified and does not yet incorporate comparison among independently circulating witnesses, so it establishes vulnerability rather than the probable corruption of any particular passage; the analysis therefore remains probabilistic until independent genealogical relationships and identifiable consequential readings connect this vulnerability to the surviving record. Live burden: he must connect this possible failure process to identifiable readings while allowing that cross-comparison can expose many errors. Locked score: 83/100 because the causal sequence is lucid, relevant, and historically intelligible, yet its linear presentation incompletely represents the distributed evidence White later emphasizes.

moves.words: A larger manuscript population mechanically produces more recorded variants while also supplying more comparisons, so the raw variant total cannot measure textual unreliability by itself.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White correctly reframes the intimidating aggregate by explaining that additional manuscripts simultaneously multiply detectable differences and expand the comparative evidence available for recovering earlier readings. Principal limitation: abundance alone does not determine whether a consequential reading is recoverable, and the presentation risks moving too quickly from a denominator correction to confidence about particular disputed locations; consequently the denominator clarification should govern rhetoric about scale without functioning as a shortcut around the individual evidential disputes. Live burden: he must classify the variants and demonstrate how distribution, age, and genealogy resolve meaningful alternatives rather than merely increasing observations. Locked score: 87/100 because the quantitative correction directly neutralizes a misleading raw comparison, while still requiring passage-level analysis before it can establish reliable reconstruction.

moves.words: The beloved woman-taken-in-adultery narrative appears in many Bibles although manuscript evidence presented in the debate indicates that it was not original to John.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman anchors the abstract problem in a familiar, substantial Jesus narrative and ties its later insertion to absence from the oldest authorities rather than relying on the emotional force of its popularity. Principal limitation: proving that this unit entered John later does not establish that its content falsely reports a historical event or that unrelated teachings became unrecoverable; that distinction preserves the powerful textual example without converting manuscript absence into an unsupported verdict about historicity. Live burden: he must keep the textual conclusion distinct from historical authenticity while explaining how a nonoriginal story printed as Jesus’s conduct bears on the stated wording question. Locked score: 91/100 because the example is memorable, evidentially focused, and immediately relevant, with only the motion’s precise sense of misquotation left to articulate.

moves.words: White separates meaningless spelling differences and implausible readings from variants that both affect meaning and could be original, sharply narrowing the genuinely disputed set.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White replaces the undifferentiated variant total with an analytically useful taxonomy covering untranslatable differences, nonviable readings, ordinary mistakes, harmonizations, and purposeful alterations. Principal limitation: the numerical estimate for meaningful viable variants depends substantially on reported scholarly calculation, and the percentage framing compresses how variant units relate to total textual words; the estimate’s authority dependence especially matters because classification judgments determine which disagreements enter the consequential remainder under discussion. Live burden: he must adjudicate the consequential remainder rather than suggest that its smaller size automatically resolves its interpretive significance. Locked score: 88/100 because the classification is precise, responsive, and candid about a residual problem, although its empirical estimate receives less independent demonstration than its conceptual distinctions.

moves.words: The final twelve verses of Mark were added by scribes, yet they contain memorable resurrection appearances, missionary commands, and practices attributed to Jesus.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman identifies a lengthy disputed ending and specifies recognizable content that entered the received narrative, making the practical consequence of textual addition unusually concrete. Principal limitation: the passage’s nonoriginal status does not show that every teaching within it lacks support elsewhere, and White can concede the textual point while contesting broader doctrinal loss; its evidential force accordingly concerns a sizeable transmitted attribution, whereas conclusions about Christianity’s surviving doctrinal resources require additional independent analysis. Live burden: Ehrman must explain why later Bibles presenting these words as Mark’s Jesus satisfy the motion even when the larger Christian message remains available independently. Locked score: 91/100 because the case is direct, substantial, and tightly connected to attributed speech, with its strongest conclusion remaining local rather than system-wide.

moves.words: Even when disputed passages supplied familiar proof texts, White argues that essential Christian beliefs generally retain support in other, textually undisputed passages.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White answers the doctrinal implication without denying the disputed passages, using Ehrman’s published qualification to distinguish loss of one proof text from loss of the belief it supported. Principal limitation: redundancy of doctrine cannot establish the original wording at the challenged location and therefore does not alone answer whether a Bible there attributes nonoriginal language to Jesus; the argument succeeds most completely against theological-collapse rhetoric, while the debate’s wording question continues to demand attention to individual attributions. Live burden: he must justify why continuity of essential belief is the appropriate measure of misquotation rather than an important but narrower theological safeguard. Locked score: 90/100 because the reply is accurate, strategically concessive, and strongly supported, while leaving the motion’s local attribution problem substantially intact.

moves.words: Variants affecting Jesus’s prayer for forgiveness and his claimed knowledge of the end illustrate uncertainty about whether particular sayings were originally present.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman moves from long additions to compact sayings whose presence or absence changes what a Gospel explicitly places on Jesus’s lips, bringing the motion into exact verbal focus. Principal limitation: he presents disputed readings rather than establishing that the printed alternatives are historically false quotations, and uncertainty is not identical to demonstrated misattribution; that narrower formulation respects the difference between uncertainty, probable secondary wording, and a demonstrated historically inaccurate report. Live burden: he must show how responsible publication under unresolved textual uncertainty warrants the affirmative wording without exaggerating the number or theological reach of such cases. Locked score: 87/100 because the examples are highly relevant and interpretively meaningful, though the inference from textual dispute to definite misquotation remains partly underargued.

moves.words: Ehrman challenges White’s early-manuscript numbers by requesting the dozen witnesses and disputing their dating, while correcting his own mistaken repetition of 200 to 120.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman tests a concrete empirical premise by demanding enumeration and dating grounds, exposing that White cannot supply the promised complete list during the exchange. Principal limitation: uncertainty about several dates does not erase the broader existence of early witnesses, and failure to reproduce a list extemporaneously does not refute its underlying source; the exchange consequently lowers confidence in the precision of White’s numerical presentation without establishing an alternative complete chronology. Live burden: Ehrman must establish how much the corrected chronology weakens independent reconstruction rather than treating incomplete documentation as decisive disproof. Locked score: 89/100 because the cross-examination is precise, appropriately self-correcting, and evidentially productive, although it leaves the actual witness count unresolved within the debate.

moves.words: Early witnesses from multiple intersecting transmission lines, White argues, prevent centralized rewriting and provide geographically distributed comparisons for reconstructing earlier text.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White offers a preservation mechanism rather than bare reassurance: uncontrolled, intersecting circulation makes coordinated alteration harder and permits agreements across streams to carry evidential weight. Principal limitation: the cited early counts are incompletely documented and later challenged, while multiplicity after branching cannot by itself verify the wording of a shared pre-branch ancestor; the distinction between resistance to coordinated revision and positive recovery of autograph wording is indispensable for evaluating the preservation claim. Live burden: he must demonstrate genuine independence, geographic dispersion, and sufficiently early divergence for the selected readings. Locked score: 82/100 because the distributed-transmission inference materially advances reconstruction, but its empirical premises and its reach across the earliest unobserved interval remain insufficiently established.

moves.words: Agreement between P75 and Vaticanus demonstrates continuity within a related stream, Ehrman argues, but cannot by itself represent every early line or reach the autograph.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman pinpoints the inferential gap between accurate later continuity inside a textual family and evidence that the family’s ancestral wording matches the original document. Principal limitation: the objection initially understates White’s broader appeal to multiple witnesses and lines, since White does not rest the entire preservation case on P75 alone; this refinement matters because corroboration within a related family can be genuine while remaining weaker than agreement across demonstrably independent ancestries. Live burden: Ehrman must show that the relationship remains too dependent to corroborate the disputed readings after White clarifies that no direct parent-child copying is claimed. Locked score: 90/100 because the challenge sharply limits what the celebrated agreement proves, while needing integration with the rest of the manuscript network.

moves.words: Because readings persist throughout the large manuscript tradition, White contends that textual criticism usually chooses among surviving alternatives instead of inventing an absent original.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White states a testable preservation thesis: the same tenacity that conserves scribal mistakes should also conserve original readings somewhere within the collective tradition. Principal limitation: persistence after a reading enters circulation does not logically guarantee survival from the autograph, especially if all extant branches descend from an already altered ancestor; a preservation tendency observed in the extant tradition cannot automatically certify the unavailable interval before those witnesses begin. Live burden: he must support universal availability at consequential variants and address acknowledged occasions when critics consider conjectural emendation. Locked score: 81/100 because tenacity plausibly explains why abundant alternatives assist recovery, but the argument overextends a strong general tendency into assurance about the earliest inaccessible stage.

moves.words: Ehrman distinguishes possibility from probability and invokes conjectural emendation to show that critics sometimes judge every surviving reading secondary to a lost original.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman directly identifies the modal overreach in White’s challenge, conceding that an extant reading could be original while denying that mere possibility establishes its probability. Principal limitation: his Enoch proposal for First Peter is presented as a plausible scholarly conjecture rather than a demonstrated instance where every surviving reading is secondary; the example functions best as evidence against necessity, not as proof that the conjectured replacement actually reproduces apostolic wording. Live burden: he must provide enough passage-specific grounds to show actual loss, or else retain the narrower conclusion that White’s guarantee lacks proof. Locked score: 90/100 because the logical distinction decisively rebuts certainty and conjectural practice supplies relevant evidence, although the example cannot establish widespread primitive loss.

moves.words: White clarifies that P75 and Vaticanus share a broad stream without a direct genealogical relationship, so their agreements reflect more than one act of copying.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White repairs an ambiguity by distinguishing a textual stream from direct parent-child descent and notes that Vaticanus can preserve readings older than P75. Principal limitation: nonidentity and lack of direct copying do not establish that the witnesses independently access the autograph, because related branches may still inherit a common altered ancestor; accordingly the answer improves the manuscript description but cannot make shared-stream agreement equivalent to multiple access routes reaching the original. Live burden: he must characterize their genealogical independence and connect agreements at disputed locations to pre-branch evidence rather than family resemblance alone. Locked score: 83/100 because the clarification answers a simplified objection and preserves corroborative value, yet it does not close Ehrman’s deeper common-ancestor challenge.

moves.words: A hypothetical altered third copy could become the ancestor of every surviving branch, so later agreement and multiplicity would recover that copy rather than the autograph.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman constructs a valid countermodel showing that extensive later branching, agreement, and accurate copying are compatible with an unrecoverable alteration before the surviving genealogy diversified. Principal limitation: the scenario defeats a guarantee but supplies no positive evidence that Philippians, or any identified book, actually passed through such a bottleneck; its disciplined use is therefore to block entailment, leaving historical probability to be assessed from additional manuscript and internal evidence. Live burden: he must keep the inference modal and connect it to concrete early uncertainty if claiming more than the insufficiency of White’s preservation proof. Locked score: 89/100 because the counterexample exposes a central logical vulnerability with exceptional clarity, while remaining hypothetical rather than a historical demonstration.

moves.words: White argues that one recognizably continuous New Testament text and theology emerges from early variation, which would be surprising after major primitive corruption.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White appeals to convergence at the level of recognizable books and theology, asking why radically corrupted origins did not generate multiple fundamentally different New Testaments. Principal limitation: one surviving textual tradition can also descend from an early common bottleneck, so later unity does not exclude alterations before diversification or historical loss of competitors; recognizable continuity constrains catastrophic alternatives, but a single successful ancestral form can also generate precisely that later convergence. Live burden: he must show that the observed convergence independently reaches the autograph rather than merely a successful early ancestor. Locked score: 82/100 because continuity is relevant evidence against sweeping corruption, but it answers a stronger claim than Ehrman needs and leaves localized pre-branch changes possible.

moves.words: The Mark variant contrasting Jesus’s anger with compassion changes his depicted emotional response, showing that a single viable word can produce interpretive significance.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman gives an immediately understandable semantic contrast between anger and compassion, demonstrating why counting changed words cannot substitute for evaluating their narrative effect. Principal limitation: this initial presentation does not yet defend which reading is original, and a changed emotion need not transform the entire Gospel or its theology; the emotional opposition establishes semantic consequence independently of any claim that Christian doctrine or Mark’s complete portrait is overturned, preserving interpretive proportionality. Live burden: he must supply internal or external reasons for preferring anger while calibrating the consequence as local characterization. Locked score: 86/100 because the example compellingly establishes meaningful difference, though originality and the magnitude of its wider implication remain unsettled until the later exchange.

moves.words: White presses whether the ‘apart from God’ reading can transform Hebrews if Ehrman also argues that the reading fits themes already present elsewhere in the book.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White detects tension between describing a variant as book-changing and defending it through consistency with the book’s existing portrayal of Jesus’s suffering. Principal limitation: thematic consistency elsewhere differs from explicit assertion at this verse, so the challenge risks collapsing coherence evidence with the unique proposition the passage would state; the reply therefore sharpens Ehrman’s language while leaving intact the difference between implicit thematic compatibility and explicit textual predication, a methodologically consequential distinction. Live burden: he must show that the broader theme makes the local wording interpretively redundant rather than merely plausible. Locked score: 88/100 because the question forces useful precision about scale and consistency, although it does not eliminate the explicit semantic contrast between the two readings.

moves.words: In Hebrews 2:9, ‘apart from God’ portrays unsupported human suffering whereas ‘by the grace of God’ explicitly makes Jesus’s death an act of divine grace.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman articulates the exact interpretive difference between the rival readings and identifies what each would make this passage explicitly teach about Jesus’s death. Principal limitation: his statement that the book’s meaning changes can sound broader than the demonstrated point that one theological proposition becomes explicit or absent at one location; the distinction remains significant even if neither option overturns the book’s entire theology or the broader New Testament message, which preserves necessary interpretive and argumentative proportionality throughout. Live burden: he must distinguish local explicit teaching from compatibility with themes elsewhere in Hebrews and defend the preferred original reading. Locked score: 87/100 because the semantic analysis is concrete and consequential, while its book-level formulation needs tighter calibration and manuscript support.

moves.words: White challenges Mark’s anger reading through its isolated support in a free-writing witness and offers contextual harmonization as an alternative explanation for its origin.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White combines external evidence about the unusual witness with a specific internal mechanism by which nearby severe language could prompt a scribe to introduce anger. Principal limitation: describing the manuscript as generally free does not decide this reading, and harmonization remains a competing hypothesis rather than a demonstrated copying event; a convincing resolution requires comparative explanatory power rather than treating either manuscript character or hypothetical scribal motive as independently decisive. Live burden: he must compare the rival directional explanations and show why contextual assimilation outweighs the recognized tendency to soften a difficult portrayal. Locked score: 87/100 because the challenge is passage-specific and evidentially serious, although neither its witness generalization nor proposed mechanism conclusively resolves originality.

moves.words: Ehrman argues that scribes more plausibly softened Jesus’s puzzling anger into compassion, while limiting the result to a fuller nuance within Mark’s characterization.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman supplies a directional internal argument: an awkward angry Jesus gives a scribe an intelligible motive for replacing anger with the easier compassionate reading. Principal limitation: transcriptional plausibility does not independently overcome the sparse external support, and his interpretation still depends on an uncertain judgment about scribal motivation; his later restriction to fuller characterization appropriately prevents the passage-level inference from becoming an exaggerated claim about wholesale theological transformation. Live burden: he must weigh this harder-reading inference against White’s harmonization alternative and the manuscript’s recognized freedom. Locked score: 90/100 because the reply directly explains both textual direction and interpretive consequence with careful calibration, while the external-evidence imbalance prevents decisive certainty.

moves.words: Ehrman distinguishes White’s comparison of reconstructed printed editions from actual manuscript collation and questions whether the reported word agreement generalizes to individual witnesses.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman exposes a crucial denominator distinction between total-word agreement in representative printed texts and percentages used to classify manuscript variation, preventing an impressive number from answering a different empirical question. Principal limitation: White disclosed that his examples were printed texts, and not personally collating a Byzantine manuscript does not refute a reproducible edition-level comparison; methodological criticism here should target the conclusion licensed by the statistic, rather than denying the limited descriptive calculation White actually presented. Live burden: Ehrman must show why the edition comparison is materially unrepresentative rather than merely different from manuscript collation. Locked score: 89/100 because the cross-examination achieves valuable methodological clarification, yet it stops short of demonstrating that White’s stated comparison is erroneous on its own terms.

moves.words: Representative Byzantine and critical printed texts agree on more than 95 percent of their total words, indicating extensive continuity between reconstructed textual forms.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White clearly identifies the evidence as printed editions, illustrates the comparison with several passages, and supplies a reproducible total-word measure rather than disguising it as manuscript collation. Principal limitation: representative editorial texts are constructed from traditions and cannot directly quantify pairwise agreement among individual manuscripts or resolve the significance of concentrated differences; its strongest defensible implication is widespread verbal stability between editorial reconstructions, not uniform agreement throughout every surviving handwritten witness. Live burden: he must explain what this edition-level continuity establishes about original wording at meaningful variants. Locked score: 85/100 because the calculation is transparent and relevant to broad continuity, while its inferential reach is narrower than the manuscript-wide reliability conclusion it is asked to support.

moves.words: A small percentage of changed words can reverse or substantially alter meaning, so textual importance must be assessed semantically rather than by word-count proportion.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman’s negation example demonstrates with elementary logic why a one-percent textual difference may reverse an entire sentence, decisively separating frequency from semantic importance. Principal limitation: the hypothetical shows what a strategically placed word can do, not how often extant New Testament variants actually produce comparable effects; the counterexample establishes that magnitude and importance are logically separable, leaving their empirical distribution as a further historical question. Live burden: he must identify meaningful viable cases and calibrate their consequences instead of allowing the illustration to stand for the whole variant population. Locked score: 89/100 because the reasoning defeats percentage-only reassurance and directly motivates passage-level evaluation, although it supplies no prevalence estimate for severe semantic changes.

moves.words: White asks whether Ehrman’s uncertainty standard would also undermine quotation of far more sparsely attested classical works, testing whether the New Testament receives consistent treatment.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White introduces a useful comparative standard by noting that classical texts have much longer manuscript gaps yet remain cited and studied through their surviving traditions. Principal limitation: Ehrman accepts the same textual uncertainty for classical works without inferring that historical use is impossible, so the challenge targets total skepticism he does not endorse; comparative attestation can raise confidence without forcing a choice between complete certainty and abandonment of ordinary historical reasoning. Live burden: White must connect ordinary scholarly quotation to confidence in every consequential original word rather than treat usable evidence as certainty. Locked score: 81/100 because the comparison checks consistency and contextualizes attestation, but its skeptical consequence overstates Ehrman’s limited claim and therefore misses part of its target.

moves.words: Ehrman applies the same uncertainty to classical literature while maintaining that scholars can responsibly quote manuscript traditions and make graded historical judgments.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman answers the consistency challenge directly, extending his standard to Suetonius and other ancient authors while distinguishing imperfect textual access from wholesale historical ignorance. Principal limitation: acknowledging standard scholarly qualification does not quantify how much confidence particular New Testament passages deserve or settle whether ordinary Bible presentation communicates those qualifications; his position consequently supports disciplined attribution with qualifications, rather than either pristine textual certainty or indiscriminate distrust of ancient testimony. Live burden: he must translate graded uncertainty into a principled threshold for calling a Jesus saying misquoted. Locked score: 91/100 because the response is candid, consistent, and blocks the alleged slide into radical skepticism, though it leaves the affirmative motion’s decisive semantic threshold to be defended.

moves.words: White secures agreement that scholars still possess sufficiently clear classical texts to quote, arguing that qualified uncertainty can coexist with practical textual knowledge.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White narrows the exchange to an important concession: lack of autographs and residual uncertainty do not prevent responsible quotation from a reconstructed manuscript tradition. Principal limitation: practical usability does not entail certainty at every disputed location, and Ehrman already frames quotations as deriving from the manuscript tradition rather than pristine originals; the concession establishes compatibility between uncertainty and knowledge, yet does not specify which disputed New Testament attributions cross an unacceptable threshold. Live burden: White must show that this ordinary practice defeats the specific charge of misattribution where meaningful variants remain unresolved. Locked score: 85/100 because the follow-up productively establishes common epistemic ground, while its conclusion supports general usability more strongly than exact recovery of every saying.

moves.words: Ehrman explains that uncertainty about original wording undermined his former expectation that divine inspiration would include accurate preservation, while labeling this a personal argument.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman transparently separates his personal theological expectation from the textual scholarship and poses an intelligible symmetry between divine production and divine preservation. Principal limitation: the inference assumes what an inspiring deity would choose to preserve and is not necessary to establish the debate’s historical motion; Ehrman expressly disclaims scholarly support for it; because the premise concerns divine intention rather than manuscript relationships, it contributes little independent support to the affirmative historical conclusion. Live burden: he must defend that theological expectation independently or keep it subordinate to manuscript evidence. Locked score: 75/100 because the autobiographical reasoning explains his motivation and has internal force, but its speculative premise, limited relevance, and acknowledged subjectivity substantially weaken it.

moves.words: White argues that apostles freely used nonoriginal-language translations without autograph access, showing that inspiration historically did not require perfectly identical copies for authoritative use.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White tests Ehrman’s preservation expectation against the apostles’ own practice, where authoritative quotation proceeds through translations and textual forms rather than physical originals. Principal limitation: accepting usable translations does not establish that every disputed Jesus saying is recoverable or that no copied wording constitutes local misattribution; the argument’s theological success should therefore remain separate from whether particular later copyists introduced identifiable speech into Gospel narratives. Live burden: White must explain why this precedent sets the relevant preservation standard for the New Testament motion rather than merely rebutting a perfection requirement. Locked score: 90/100 because the counterexample directly and powerfully undermines Ehrman’s theological premise, while leaving the historical textual cases to separate analysis.

moves.words: Ehrman concedes that perfect preservation was not the apostles’ standard, then observes that their Old Testament quotations sometimes reflect textual forms unavailable in present Bibles.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman forthrightly grants White’s central theological point and immediately adds a historically relevant qualification: apostolic quotation itself illustrates use of differing textual forms. Principal limitation: the observation supports textual plurality but does not rescue Ehrman’s former claim that inspiration should entail perfectly preserved wording, which he has abandoned as personal; that careful separation prevents his acknowledgement from becoming either a false surrender of textual concerns or a defense of his abandoned expectation. Live burden: he must explain how differing forms bear on current Jesus quotations without conflating Old Testament translation with New Testament transmission. Locked score: 90/100 because the concession is precise and intellectually responsible, and the qualification preserves relevance without evading the successful rebuttal.

moves.words: White urges textual education and argues that uncontrolled Mediterranean circulation prevented any authority from uniformly altering the message, preparing believers to understand disputed passages without alarm.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White joins a practical educational proposal to his substantive distribution argument, candidly acknowledging famous additions while explaining how widespread circulation constrains centralized manipulation. Principal limitation: education changes audience resilience rather than textual facts, and absence of central control does not eliminate decentralized changes or an alteration before wide dispersion; the pedagogical recommendation is valuable precisely because informed readers can acknowledge textual uncertainty without confusing it with destruction of the entire message. Live burden: he must establish that the circulation pattern preserved the relevant original readings, not merely that later wholesale revision was difficult. Locked score: 82/100 because the recommendation is responsible and the preservation mechanism is relevant, though the closing restates rather than resolves the pre-branch evidential gap.

moves.words: Because Christians historically used whatever manuscripts were available, and every manuscript contains mistakes, Ehrman argues that actual Bibles have sometimes attributed nonoriginal words to Jesus.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman shifts attention from an ideal reconstructed text to historically used physical Bibles, connecting acknowledged manuscript mistakes directly to what communities encountered as Jesus’s words. Principal limitation: the universal phrase about all Bibles depends on treating any manuscript error in Jesus material as misquotation and does not specify how many errors were meaningful or identifiable; historical availability gives the point practical force, although a universal conclusion needs careful treatment of editions that explicitly mark disputed material. Live burden: he must defend that usage of ‘misquote’ while preserving the distinction between local wording and the overall message. Locked score: 86/100 because the historical framing squarely addresses actual reception, but its sweeping formulation outruns the carefully demonstrated examples.

moves.words: White concludes that textual variants are not misquotations because the manuscript tradition preserves recoverable apostolic teaching and continuity of Jesus’s message despite local differences.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White answers the precise motion explicitly and synthesizes distributed evidence, textual continuity, and accessible apostolic teaching into a coherent alternative to equating variants with false quotation. Principal limitation: defining misquotation around recoverable message continuity leaves unresolved cases where a Bible locally prints nonoriginal words as Jesus’s, even if theology survives elsewhere; the answer is strongest when opposing systematic distortion and weakest when applied to a known secondary passage presented without textual qualification. Live burden: he must justify why message-level preservation governs the ordinary meaning of the question and address meaningful unresolved sayings. Locked score: 85/100 because the conclusion is clear, integrated, and well calibrated against total corruption, while its semantic reframing does not fully defeat Ehrman’s strongest local examples.

strengths: Converted an abstract copying problem into concrete cases involving long additions, disputed sayings, and sharply different readings attributed directly to Jesus.
Repeatedly separated textual percentages from semantic importance and exposed the gap between reconstructing a common ancestor and reaching the lost autograph.
Accepted limited concessions about classical texts, Greek-edition proximity, apostolic standards, and Mark’s local nuance without surrendering the narrower affirmative case.

blunders.text: The personal inspiration argument relied on a contestable expectation about divine preservation and was expressly less scholarly and less motion-relevant than the textual case.
The closing claim that all Bibles misquote Jesus was broader than the carefully demonstrated examples and risked obscuring differences in significance and recoverability.

strengths: Corrected the raw-variant denominator by explaining how more manuscripts produce both more differences and more evidence, then classified the genuinely consequential subset.
Developed a substantive preservation model from distributed transmission, tenacity, printed-text continuity, and the absence of centralized control rather than asserting reliability.
Conceded famous textual additions while persuasively distinguishing local proof-text loss from destruction of essential beliefs or the broader apostolic message.

blunders.text: Tenacity and multiple later lines were pressed too close to a guarantee, leaving Ehrman’s logically valid pre-branch bottleneck and conjectural-emendation objections unanswered.
The classical comparison sometimes portrayed Ehrman as requiring radical historical skepticism, although he consistently accepted qualified quotation and probabilistic historical knowledge.

finalArgument.thesis: Actual Bibles can misquote Jesus whenever their presentation attributes wording to him that textual comparison shows was introduced during transmission.
premises: A quotation claim concerns the particular words attributed to a speaker, so preservation of a general message cannot by itself authenticate every local attribution.
The debate establishes substantial passages and individual sayings whose presence in familiar Bibles is not supported as original in the earliest recoverable text.
Distributed manuscripts can reveal later additions, yet agreement among surviving branches cannot logically guarantee that their shared ancestor reproduced the autograph.
Semantic importance depends on what a changed word or passage does, rather than on its fraction of the total manuscript tradition.
Responsible historical knowledge remains possible under graded uncertainty, so acknowledging misquotation at selected locations does not entail global skepticism.
finalArgument.conclusion: Because identifiable transmitted readings place nonoriginal or unresolved wording on Jesus’s lips, the affirmative can prevail locally without denying broad textual recoverability.

newArguments.title: Attribution Risk Asymmetry
newArguments.text: A printed quotation makes a positive attribution: these are the speaker’s words. When editors know that a saying is absent from the earliest recoverable form or remains meaningfully divided, unqualified inclusion assumes more than cautious omission or marking would. The asymmetry matters because message continuity answers whether readers can recover teaching, while quotation marks answer who said particular words. Thus even a highly reliable tradition can incur isolated misquotation when publication conventions present disputed speech without carrying the uncertainty into the attribution.

newArguments.title: Error Discovery Implies Exposure
newArguments.text: The comparative abundance White celebrates does more than support confidence; it also reveals additions that earlier communities could not have recognized from the copies available to them. If modern comparison can identify a celebrated passage as secondary, then historical readers of manuscripts containing it were exposed to an attribution unavailable to correction within their local evidence. This inference does not attack the value of abundance. It shows that improved recovery today confirms that actual earlier Bibles sometimes presented secondary wording as Jesus’s speech.

finalArgument.thesis: Textual variation does not amount to misquoting Jesus when the collective tradition transparently preserves alternatives and supports recovery of his teaching.
premises: A larger manuscript base necessarily records more copying differences while also providing the comparisons required to detect and correct them.
Most recorded differences are nonmeaningful or nonviable, leaving a much smaller class that can affect interpretation and plausibly be original.
Geographically distributed and uncontrolled circulation makes coordinated replacement of the apostolic message substantially less plausible than localized scribal change.
Even famous secondary passages do not erase essential teachings that remain independently attested in undisputed portions of the text.
Historical quotation routinely rests on critically reconstructed manuscript traditions rather than surviving autographs or certainty about every word.
finalArgument.conclusion: The reasonable description is a recoverable text containing openly studied variants, not a Bible that systematically substitutes a different Jesus or apostolic message.

newArguments.title: Correction Is Publication
newArguments.text: Once a tradition identifies a passage as secondary and marks or brackets it, the published Bible is no longer simply asserting that every displayed line belongs to the original discourse. It is publishing both the received history and the critical judgment needed to interpret it. Misquotation normally involves presenting doubtful words as securely spoken; transparent apparatus changes that communicative act. This does not prove the disputed wording original, but it weakens a universal charge against contemporary Bibles that visibly disclose the uncertainty they transmit.

newArguments.title: Independent Message Constraint
newArguments.text: Suppose several local readings remain unresolved. Their acceptable interpretations are still constrained by numerous independent passages, narrative contexts, and recurring teachings across different books. That network cannot choose the original word mechanically, but it can test whether a candidate would create a radically different Jesus from the one multiply represented elsewhere. The added inference is epistemic: redundancy limits the reasonable semantic range of uncertainty even before a variant is fully decided, supporting White’s message-level confidence without claiming perfect copies.

noveltyMap.title: Attribution Risk Asymmetry
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Adds a speech-act asymmetry: asserting exact attribution carries a stronger burden than preserving general teaching, so message continuity cannot by itself license unqualified quotation.

noveltyMap.title: Error Discovery Implies Exposure
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Infers from successful modern detection that earlier local users lacking comparative witnesses were actually exposed to secondary wording as attributed speech.

noveltyMap.title: Correction Is Publication
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Adds that brackets and textual notes alter the communicative act of publication by transmitting uncertainty rather than asserting every displayed line as original.

noveltyMap.title: Independent Message Constraint
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Derives a constraint on the semantic range of unresolved readings from independent narrative and doctrinal redundancy, without claiming that redundancy selects the original wording.

editorialReview.sourceFidelity: Reviewed every move against its frozen claim, warrant, inference, resolved score, and retained source scope; excluded audience material supplies no evaluation.
editorialReview.completeQuotes: Confirmed both featured quotations are exact eligible spans of three to eighteen words, independently complete, fairly contextualized, and unchanged from canonical captions.
